newsitem.title: ITALY: Left leader warns Italy government over pensions.
newsitem.headline: Left leader warns Italy government over pensions.

text.p: The leader of the hard-left party that guarantees the Italian government's parliamentary majority on Tuesday warned the coalition that it risked its very survival if pension reforms disregarded workers' rights.
"Early pensions cannot be touched," Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said in an interview in Milan's Corriere Della Sera newspaper.
Bertinotti said tampering with the rights of workers to retire early if they have accrued enough years of service and contributions to state funds would be discriminatory.

"If the government decides to go against (the rights of) workers it must understand that it risks its survival," said Bertinotti, whose party holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament.
Prodi's centre-left government almost fell in April when Refoundation refused to back a security force for Albania.

Workers in Italy are allowed to retire before the age of 63 for men and 60 for women if they have accrued enough years of contributions. This is usually between 25 and 30 years in the public sector and and 35 years in the private sector.
Known as "pensioni di anzianita", or pensions based on length of service, they have put strain on successive governments' budgets because state payouts must begin some 10 or 15 years early.

The future of such pensions came to a political head on Monday when Massimo D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), said Italy could not go on with the current system, which he said was "unsustainable".
"When there is mass unemployment, especially among the young in the south, we can't allow ourselves to pay pensions at 50 or 52 years of age," D'Alema told a conference.
"This system is increasingly unsustainable. We have to get out of it, it's the only way," said D'Alema, whose party is the largest force in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition.
Bertinotti's warning came in response to D'Alema's comments, which the Italian media saw as a political watershed because the alarm was being sounded by the country's top leftist.
"Pensions: a turning point for D'Alema," headlined Rome's La Repubblica newspaper.
D'Alema said the 1998 budget would include structural reform of the pensions system and the government was working to that end.
Bertinotti said changes in italy's pension system could be decided now but that the effects of the reform should not be felt until 2008, when forecasts show the system will hit a liquidity crisis.
"In talking about the welfare state, pensions are the last item to talk about," Bertinotti said.
A hold-down on early retirements could bring big savings for the cash-strapped Treasury as Italy fights to control state spending to meet targets for the European single currency.
State pensions body Inps has reported a recent surge in requests for early retirements from various sectors amid rising fears of a government crackdown on pension benefits.

Italy announced last week that it was limiting early retirement for teachers but government officials on Monday were quick to deny reports that it was planning to freeze early pensions throughout the civil service.
The government last week began what are expected to be lengthy talks with union leaders on welfare reform.
Economists say Italy must bite the welfare bullet to have a hope of being in economic and monetary union at its 1999 launch.
Italy spends more than any other European Union country on pension benefits and the bill is set to climb unless reforms are introduced, national statistical institute Istat said last week.
